entries.title: Trump to appeal ballroom construction halt to Supreme Court
entries.summary: A US Court of Appeals upheld a ruling that saying Trump cannot build a White House ballroom without congressional approval. The president vowed to appeal what he called an "unjust decision."
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump to appeal ballroom construction halt to Supreme Court

August 7, 2026

A US Court of Appeals upheld a ruling that saying Trump cannot build a White House ballroom without congressional approval. The president vowed to appeal what he called an "unjust decision."

US President Donald Trump was ordered on Friday to halt construction of a ballroom on the site of the demolished East Wing. 

The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld a preliminary injunction won by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which had sued Trump over the matter last year.

It was a major setback for Trump, who has touted the project, saying the White House needed a large ballroom to host events.

The court's ruling has been placed on hold for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal the ruling to the US Supreme Court.

Trump confirmed the move, saying his team will be "immediately appealing" to the Supreme Court.

The US president blasted the decision as a "horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful ruling."

"The Circuit Court also refused to acknowledge that the desperately needed, and totally secure Ballroom, which is being built ahead of schedule and under budget, is a Gift from President Trump and Great Patriots of the United States of America," Trump added in a social media post.

What did the court say?

Judges Patricia Millett and Brad Garcia, both appointed by Democratic presidents, said the ‌order does not permanently bar construction of the ballroom, but rather it merely halts above-ground work during the lawsuit and until the White House secures approval from Congress.

"Each President is a temporary tenant, not the ‌owner, of the White House" ⁠and ⁠cannot fundamentally reshape it without congressional approval, the court said.

"Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the panel's majority wrote. "Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People's House — to fit a particular ‌President's desires."

Additionally, the court scolded "the bold assertion that the Executive can act with utter lawlessness, destroying treasured national landmarks and harming the interests of individuals."

Court rejects 'national security' argument

Work on the 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom began last year with the swift demolition of the White House's entire historic East Wing. It is the biggest structural change to the White House in over 70 years.

White House lawyers argued that the ballroom includes critical security features to guard against a range of threats, such as drones, ballistic missiles and biohazards.

"These upgrades, alterations, and improvements are essential to protecting the President, his family, and his staff, as well as the White House itself, and the entire project flows from them," government attorneys told the court.

But the justices in the majority shot down the argument, saying that national security arguments "are not an automatic get-out-of-law-free card."

entries.title: Ceuta: Spain warns Italy it will reciprocate entry checks
entries.summary: Spain has told Italy it will impose entry checks on visitors unless Rome halts its controls by Sunday. Even though they don't share a land border, the countries entered a spat after the Ceuta border rush.
entries.content:
Spain

Ceuta: Spain warns Italy it will reciprocate entry checks

August 7, 2026

Spain has told Italy it will impose entry checks on visitors unless Rome halts its controls by Sunday. Even though they don't share a land border, the countries entered a spat after the Ceuta border rush.

Spain's government on Friday threatened to impose reciprocal entry checks on travelers from Italy, unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's governemnt lifts the measures it has implemented by Sunday. 

Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week. 

The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes.

Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy.

What did Spain say about possible checks on travelers from Italy?

Spain called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population." 

Madrid had objected to the move on several grounds, saying it was based on "spurious arguments."

It said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years. 

"If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said.

Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15.

Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zoneamid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however.

What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain?

Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground.

Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure.

"They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers."

Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities.

"I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough."

Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration

At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration.

Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe.

Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market.

Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare.

"Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years."

entries.title: How viable is the potential Iran-Oman Hormuz shipping deal?
entries.summary: Iran says a shipping accord with Oman is in its final stages, but analysts warn sanctions, security concerns and rival US-Iran goals could limit its impact.
entries.content:
Iran

How viable is the potential Iran-Oman Hormuz shipping deal?

August 7, 2026

Iran says a shipping accord with Oman is in its final stages, but analysts warn sanctions, security concerns and rival US-Iran goals could limit its impact.

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, said this week that an agreement with Oman, which lies on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz, is in the "final stage" of review and drafting — provided that no external party interfered in the process.

The two Persian Gulf states have agreed on the geographical coordinates of a navigation route through the strait, Baghaei was quoted as saying by state news agency IRNA on Wednesday evening.

Baghaei told journalists that even if an understanding was reached, it would not mean that the strait had become safe for all passing vessels.

"The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States, particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests," he said.

What the agreement could look like

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi also said an agreement on new shipping arrangements was nearing completion, IRNA reported.

Gharibabadi stressed that the proposed arrangement would not amount to a full reopening of the strait, but would instead establish a new model for maritime traffic.

According to IRNA, Gharibabadi said the route would be temporary and could remain open for between two and four months.

Tehran said that any reopening of the strait must be accompanied by an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports.

Reports cited by Agence France-Presse (AFP) said Iran was planning to block US and Israeli ships from the waterway as part of a deal with Oman.

Iran also argued that vessels passing through the strait should pay fees for safe passage. Oman did not support unilateral Iranian control of the waterway.

Obstacles and skepticism

A proposed deal between Iran and Oman to give Tehran control over ships entering the Persian Gulf ​through the Strait ⁠of Hormuz is not easily workable because of US sanctions and restrictive insurance clauses ⁠on payments, according to industry sources cited by Reuters on Friday.

However, analysts cautioned that any deal on the reopening of the strait should be viewed as a tactical pause rather than a durable settlement.

Security analyst Shukriya Bradost told DW such a pause could benefit Washington more than Tehran.

"The United States could use the period to improve coordination with its regional partners, review its military strategy and prepare stronger options," she said.

"Iran, meanwhile, would continue facing economic pressure, internal divisions and growing political and security costs."

"If this period becomes merely a pause in tensions and Tehran fails to secure a tangible strategic gain, the passage of time may benefit the United States more than any other party," Bradost added.

Other analysts pointed to fundamental disagreements over the future governance of the waterway.

Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, said Tehran and Washington are pursuing different objectives.

"Iran wants control over vessels entering the strait, while the United States wants completely free passage," Dorbeiki told DW. "These positions cannot easily be reconciled."

Competing views of Iran's role in Hormuz

Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, said both Tehran and Washington could potentially present a deal as a tactical success.

From Iran's perspective, he said any understanding could be presented as an achievement.

"The regime has not collapsed, its missile capabilities remain intact, enriched uranium has not left the country, and for the first time since the war, Iran has reinforced its leverage over the inbound shipping lane of the strait," he told DW.

Salavati added that Tehran could claim domestically that it has preserved the strategic leverage of the Strait of Hormuz.

He said the United States could also portray the situation as a success in the form of "relief from the pressure of soaring energy prices, an opportunity to replenish weapons stockpiles while easing pressure on defence production, and the ability to declare an end to the active phase of the war."

Salavati suggested that Tehran is unlikely to regard any arrangement as the end of the broader confrontation.

Trump has faced pressure from members of his own party in Congress to bring the conflict to a close before November's midterm elections.

Oman has not publicly commented on the reported agreement, which Iran says was negotiated without US involvement.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Berlin clubs struggle as drink sales dry up and costs rise
entries.summary: Berlin's clubs are still drawing crowds, but shorter nights, fewer alcohol sales and rising costs have changed their business model. Door fees, rather than bar takings, are increasingly their real financial lifeline.
entries.content:
August 7, 2026

Berlin's clubs are still drawing crowds, but shorter nights, fewer alcohol sales and rising costs have changed their business model. Door fees, rather than bar takings, are increasingly their real financial lifeline.

Berlin's world-famous club scene has remained in high demand, but venues are increasingly struggling to turn packed dancefloors into sustainable businesses.

A major survey released on Friday found that club revenue has shifted dramatically away from drinks and toward admission fees.

What's happened to Berlin's clubs?

The shift reflects changing nightlife habits since 2017, when around 60% of revenue came from food and drink sales and just 21% from entry fees.

Today, ticket sales account for 59% of revenue, while food and drink generate just 20%.

"People are planning their club nights more consciously, staying for shorter periods, and drinking less,” according to the report, the first comprehensive study of the sector since 2019.

Some 73% of respondents said alcohol consumption was falling, while 60% reported rising demand for non-alcoholic drinks and 57% said guests were staying for shorter periods.

At the same time, costs are rising.

Staff costs were cited as a major burden by 64% of respondents, operating costs by 62%, customers' declining purchasing power by 60%, and rents and leases by 54%.

Some 85% of the clubs polled said financial pressure was already changing their event programs.

Is running a Berlin club lucrative?

Demand remains strong, with 83% of clubs and event organizers reporting occupancy rates of at least 50% and around a third exceeding 75%.

But fewer venues are making enough money to cover their costs.

In 2017, 79% were at least breaking even. By 2025, that figure had dropped to 61%.

Some 39% ended the year in the red, compared with 21% in 2017.

The number of smaller operators has also risen sharply. Some 45% now generate less than €100,000 ($115,595) in annual revenue, compared with 16% in 2017.

Long-term insecurity remains another major problem. Only 8% of operators own their venues, while 31% have rental or lease agreements lasting less than five years.

How are clubs adapting?

Some 23% of respondents said they were considering closing their business within the next 12 months. Since 2020, at least 24 club and cultural venues have closed, but around 25 new ones have opened.

Many venues have already adapted to the pressure.

Some 67% have increased drink prices, 47% have raised admission charges and 39% have expanded private rentals.

The Club Commission is calling for publicly owned buildings to be opened up for nightlife, more reliable long-term funding, formal recognition of clubs as cultural venues and better working conditions.

entries.title: Eco wins: Hungary goes solar, marmots go viral and Rome gets an upgrade
entries.summary: From Hungary's accidental solar revolution to marmot crowdfunding and a long-overdue upgrade for Rome's big snake, good news comes in strange packages this week.
entries.content:
August 7, 2026

From Hungary's accidental solar revolution to marmot crowdfunding and a long-overdue upgrade for Rome's big snake, good news comes in strange packages this week.

Hungary's former leader Viktor Orban called European Union climate policy a "utopian fantasy" and effectively banned wind turbines. And yet the country has quietly become Europe's solar leader, with 25% of its electricity now being being generated from the renewable energy source, ahead of sunnier countries like Spain, and Greece.

The boom was driven not by climate concern but by self-sufficiency politics and cheap subsidies. Now a 450-megawatt park, just east of Budapest, is due online by September 2026. It's set to power around 106,000 households. 

Marmot researchers find a new way to fund their science

When US federal funding dried up, researchers from UCLA and the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory got creative. They launched OnlyMarms: a free platform posting videos of yellow-bellied marmots eating, digging and scampering in the wild, where fans can donate to support the science.

The team has tracked individually marked marmots in Colorado since 1962, building six decades of data on family lives, social behavior and responses to environmental change — and say studying marmot hibernation could even hold clues about human aging.

Rome's 'big snake' gets a cooler future

Corviale, a kilometer-long brutalist housing complex outside Rome nicknamed "the big snake," was completed in the 1980s and has since fallen into decay. With summers in some parts of Italy's now averaging around 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), life inside has become tough for its more than 4,000 residents. 

But upgrades are coming: a new library doubling as a cooling shelter, more trees and energy efficiency improvements, all aimed at helping Corviale stay cool as temperatures keep rising.

Senegalese designer turns discarded textiles into sustainable fashion

Berlin-based designer Mame Khady Badji transforms discarded clothing into bold garments inspired by her Senegalese heritage, combining traditional Ndiakhass techniques with contemporary streetwear. Her creations have drawn musicians, performers and creatives — and recently appeared at Berlin Fashion Week 2026.

After moving to Germany in 2017, Badji built her label with support from Berlin's textile community. Now she's pursuing an ambitious goal: proving that recycled fashion can be both culturally rooted and commercially viable.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

entries.title: Thailand: Several killed in school shooting north of Bangkok
entries.summary: The shooting incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi, just north of the capital city of Bangkok. Several people were killed in the attack.
entries.content:
Published August 7, 2026last updated August 7, 2026

The shooting incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi, just north of the capital city of Bangkok. Several people were killed in the attack.

Several people were killed and others injured in a shooting at a high school in Thailand's Nonthaburi province, north of the capital city of Bangkok, local authorities said.

Students, teachers and other workers were evacuated from school as authorities deployed police officers, rescue workers and emergency doctors to the scene.

Boy accused of killing grandparents before school shooting

According to the police, the suspected gunman, who is a 14-year-old student at the school, is thought to have first fatally shot his grandparents with his grandfather's handgun. The suspect lived with his grandparents, and police found them dead behind a locked door as they began to investigate the shooting.

Authorities later revised down the total death toll. Having initially said that the suspect killed six people, including students, at the school, police later said he killed two teachers and three other adults who were staff at the school.

Officials said the suspect then took his own life at the site, in the Nonthaburi province bordering Bangkok.

Bangyai Hospital, about 5 kilometers (roughly 3 miles) from the school, said 23 people were wounded, of whom 10 were in critical condition, with most suffering gunshot wounds. Earlier reports gave conflicting casualty numbers.

Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul expressed his condolences and stated that he had instructed relevant officials to assist those affected.

"It's such a terrible incident. It should never have happened," he told reporters.

Later, Anutin said that the teenage suspect in the deadly school shooting was "under stress" and there was preliminary evidence of him planning the attack ahead of time. The prime minister also told reporters that he would discuss gun control with the country's police chief.

Students express shock

The incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi.

"I didn't think it was a gun at first," an 18-year-old student told Reuters, adding that he initially thought it could be firecrackers. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. ​Then it started again."

"I was afraid that I would die, and I was scared that I wouldn't be able to pursue my dreams," said Pawarisa Maylissa, a grade 12 student who hopes to attend medical school. "I heard many gunshots very loudly because it seemed the suspect was on the floor directly above us. I could even hear bullets hitting the floor."

According to district authorities, the Debsirin Nonthaburi School had an enrollment of around 3,100 students and 147 teachers in the 2025 academic year.

School shootings in Thailand

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. It is estimated that around 10 million firearms are in circulation, or about one for every seven people.

In February, a 17-year-old stole a gun from the police and opened fire at a public high school in southern Thailand. The two-hour attack resulted in one death and two injuries.

In October 2023, a 14-year-old opened fire at Bangkok's popular Siam Paragon shopping mall, killing two people and wounding five others. Police said the shooter used a modified pistol, originally designed to fire blanks, that had likely been bought online.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: What should Europe do about its drying rivers?
entries.summary: The Rhine and Danube have reached historic lows. Dwindling water levels are affecting shipping, agriculture and ecosystems — and raising concerns about the future of drinking water supplies.
entries.content:
August 7, 2026

The Rhine and Danube have reached historic lows. Dwindling water levels are affecting shipping, agriculture and ecosystems — and raising concerns about the future of drinking water supplies.

Following an intense heat wave in June and severe wildfires in southern France and Spain, Europe's summer of climate-fueled crises continues with rivers across the continent running low.

Parts of the vital Rhine, Danube and Po rivers have fallen to historically low levels, threatening freight transport, the wider economy, and agriculture, with farmers warning of increased prices due to poor harvests amid the drought. 

Along the Danube, cargo and cruise ships can no longer pass in some places. In Hungary, Romania and Croatia, sunken ships and cars have reemerged as riverbeds dry out. 

In German cities, including Cologne and Düsseldorf, people can now walk across parts of the Rhine where strong currents normally flow. River levels could fall even more dramatically in the coming days.

The water crisis is being intensified by global warming driven by the burning of coal, oil and gas. Low water levels are also taking a growing toll on ecosystems — and could eventually drive up the cost of clean drinking water. 

The impact on nature

Parched fields, millions of hectares of lost harvests and exposed riverbeds are among the most obvious consequences of the drought. But underwater ecosystems are suffering too.

As water levels fall, rivers become warmer and contain less dissolved oxygen, increasing the risk of fish die-offs, explained Jeanette Völker, a scientist with Germany's federal environment agency, the UBA.

"Especially along the Rhine, you can see how the gravel banks are drying up. These are habitats for mussels and invertebrates, which in turn serve as food for fish. This puts enormous stress on these ecosystems. Mussels cannot move away quickly enough and die off," Völker told DW.

Drought, intense sunshine, and high nutrient loads from agricultural fertilizers also encourage algal blooms harmful to fish.

These effects were seen in 2022 on the Oder River in eastern Germany. High temperatures, low water levels and elevated salinity allowed a toxic invasive algae to spread. Around 1,000 metric tons of fish died along parts of the German-Polish border river.

Experts do not expect a repeat of the Oder disaster on the Rhine this summer because oxygen levels remain sufficiently high. But the danger to the wider freshwater ecosystem remains.

What dwindling rivers mean for drinking water costs

The Rhine and the Danube are fed by numerous tributaries that are also running low. These tributaries are crucial because their lush, reed-filled banks act as natural filters, allowing water to slowly pass through layers of soil that help remove pollutants before water reaches underground wells.

"Much of our drinking water is what's known as 'riverbank filtration,'" said Hagen Koch, a researcher specializing in climate adaptation and resilience at Germany's Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.

In other words, Germany's drinking water comes from those wells. But drought is weakening this process. Pollutant concentrations are increasing because roughly the same volume of wastewater — largely from industry and sewage works — is discharged into rivers even as water levels fall.

"If the ecosystem is damaged — that is, the animals and plants that contribute to water purification — this results in significant additional costs. Additional treatment is needed to supply clean drinking water to millions of people," Koch told DW.

German industry groups estimate water supply costs could rise by up to 30% as a result of climate change. By 2035, additional investments of up to €14 billion could be needed for improved water treatment systems, as well as deeper mains and upgraded reservoirs designed to keep water temperatures low and limit microbial growth.

The situation has drawn attention to a broader debate over water use. While households pay for the water they consume, several industries — including mining and agriculture — are exempt from water abstraction fees in many German states.

To conserve water, authorities in some German cities are currently severely restricting withdrawal from streams and rivers by private individuals. In Cologne, residents who violate the ban face fines of up to €50,000 ($58,000).

Low water levels hitting the economy

Low water levels in Germany's rivers are already taking a significant toll on the economy. Some vessels are carrying just a fifth of their usual cargo, delaying production and driving up prices. Germany's steel, chemical and petroleum industries have been hit particularly hard.

Energy supplies are also under pressure. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has urged households and businesses to conserve electricity. He warned the country could face an unprecedented energy crisis after low water levels in the Danube forced the shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant. 

Romania blasts rocks as Europe searches for solutions

Politicians are exploring emergency measures in response to the situation. In Romania, the military blasted apart a rock formation in a branch of the Danube to secure the cooling water supply for the Cernavoda nuclear power plant and avoid a shutdown.

Germany's transport minister brought together representatives from industry, ports and inland shipping on August 6 to consider short- and long-term solutions to the crisis. One proposal under discussion was deepening parts of the Rhine's navigation channel so shipping can continue despite low water levels.

Critics warn that further dredging and deepening of shipping channels would accelerate water runoff, lower groundwater levels, and cause floodplains to dry out more quickly, ultimately do little to solve the problem in the long-term.  

Instead, they're calling for the expanded use of low-water vessels, as well as a shift from freight transport to rail. Koch supports the development of ships with shallower drafts, but notes such changes require significant time and investment.

For Jeanette Völker, the solution lies in restoring parts of Europe's heavily modified rivers. Reconnecting floodplains, protecting wetlands and restoring peatlands would help landscapes retain more water and improve resilience during future droughts.

Reservoirs and dams may also play a role where they are environmentally acceptable. But experts warn adaptation alone will not be enough. Without climate protection and a rapid reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, any investments are little more than a drop in a fast-flowing river.

This article orginally appeared in German and was translated by Josh Axelrod.

entries.title: Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing seeks legitimacy in Thailand
entries.summary: Bangkok rolled out the red carpet for the Myanmar leader, but experts say the former junta chief still faces major obstacles in his bid for regional acceptance.
entries.content:
Myanmar

Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing seeks legitimacy in Thailand

August 7, 2026

Bangkok rolled out the red carpet for the Myanmar leader, but experts say the former junta chief still faces major obstacles in his bid for regional acceptance.

Myanmar's junta chief turned president Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a two-day visit to Thailand on Friday.

His first visit to the neighboring nation as civilian leader was aimed at recasting himself as the leader of a civilian government after years of diplomatic isolation, experts told DW.

His reception on landing in Bangkok on Thursday had all the pomp and circumstance befitting a visiting head of state — red carpet, honor guard, blaring national anthems and smiling photo ops with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.

"Naypyidaw equates engagement with acceptance," said Moe Thuzar, head of the Myanmar Studies Program at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, referring to Myanmar's capital.

"Min Aung Hlaing is seeking to leverage Naypyidaw's space in bilateral relations with neighbours' specific interests to secure greater acceptance of his administration from external partners."

Since the retired general seized power in a 2021 coup that toppled a democratically elected government, a brutal civil war between the military and armed resistance groups has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced well over 3 million.

Western countries have imposed several rounds of sanctions on Min Aung Hlaing's regime over alleged war crimes and other human rights abuses, charges the government rejects.

In 2024, the then-chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing himself for crimes against humanity committed against Rohingya Muslims. 

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which traditionally emphasizes non-interference in another member's domestic affairs, has barred him or his foreign minister from attending its leaders' summits.

Hoping to break out of its growing isolation, Myanmar held staggered elections in December and January that were widely criticized by the United Nations and Western governments as a sham designed to legitimize continued military rule.  

The military-aligned Union Solidarity and Development Party won more than 80% of seats, paving the way for parliament to elect Min Aung Hlaing president in April.

What is Thailand's role in Myanmar's reengagement?

Myanmar's government rejects criticism of the electoral process, saying the elections were part of a transition to civilian rule and a return of power to the people.

Since becoming president, Hlaing has paid official visits to India, China, Laos and now Thailand, as Bangkok pushed for peace efforts in Myanmar's civil war and its reengagement with ASEAN.

"For Min Aung Hlaing, visiting Thailand is also [about] finding legitimacy in the ASEAN region, because Thailand is a … founder of ASEAN and has [a] big voice in ASEAN," said Wai Yan Phyo Naing, a visiting scholar at Taiwan's Academia Sinica who studies Myanmar.

"He can show the [other] ASEAN members that Thailand is treating me like this, Laos already treated me like this. So, do you want to [act] based on the realistic point of view, or are you still wanting to argue I'm not the legitimate leader of Myanmar?" he said.

Moe Thuzar and Wai Yan Phyo Naing both agree that the bloc, which did not officially endorse Myanmar's last elections, like most countries, was not likely to let Min Aung Hlaing back to its leaders' summits any time soon.

ASEAN still insists that Myanmar first make meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that they all agreed to a few months after the coup, a plan Hlaing has dismissed repeatedly, most recently last week.

Still, Min Aung Hlaing may be hoping that his official trips abroad as newly installed president

help convince ASEAN to accept his government "on its own terms," Moe Thuzar added.

Either way, she said, Min Aung Hlaing will use his trip to Thailand to build on the bilateral relationship between the neighbors, which share a 2,400 kilometer (1,490-mile) land border.

The visit included a business forum on Thursday for Thai and Myanmar firms.

"The focus on trade and economic deals reflects Naypyidaw's and Bangkok's interest in prioritising economic engagement and addressing concerns related to border trade," said Moe Thuzar.

The economics of legitimacy

Thailand is among Myanmar's top trade partners and foreign investors, including in energy projects vital to both. A Thai firm operates two of Myanmar's main gas fields, which supply much of Thailand's natural gas.

David Mathieson, an independent Myanmar analyst based in Thailand, says convincing those investors to stay, or new ones to come in, helps shore up support for Hlaing among a key constituency.

Regardless of the ex-general's official title, he said, "he's a military dictator, and to be a dictator you need a certain level of cooperation, and cooperation comes from economic elites."

"He's appealing to an incredibly cynical international system that's like, hey, you did this. None of us buy it, but it's good enough for us. You dressed up for the party, well done, and [it's] business as usual," Mathieson said.

"Does that help the 54 million people of Myanmar? No, it doesn't. It helps him and it helps the system that props him up."

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Germany: Far-right AfD extends its lead in nationwide polls
entries.summary: In the latest Sunday poll, the AfD continues to pull ahead. And more and more people are against excluding the right-wing populists from decision-making, at least on a case-by-case basis.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Far-right AfD extends its lead in nationwide polls

August 7, 2026

In the latest Sunday poll, the AfD continues to pull ahead. And more and more people are against excluding the right-wing populists from decision-making, at least on a case-by-case basis.

For the time being, there is still widespread agreement among all democratic parties in Germany: Cooperating with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) remains out of the question. However, whether this will remain the case is becoming increasingly uncertain. The established parties have so far been unable to halt the AfD's surge in the polls over recent months.

This has also been confirmed by the latest ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey conducted by the polling firm infratest-dimap. One thousand three hundred eligible voters were asked what party they would vote for if a federal election were held next Sunday, and 28% said they would vote for the AfD. This represents a one-percentage-point increase and a new record high for the AfD in the monthly polly.

In contrast, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party, the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), and its sister party, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU), have seen a slight decline compared to the last poll in early July while all other parties have maintained their previous levels.

A clear majority supports reaching out to the AfD

In September, state elections will take place in two important eastern German states: Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In both states, the AfD leads in the polls. In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling at 41% and might be able to govern alone, if the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) fails to cross the 5% threshhold for representation in parliament.

However, only 37% of voters across Germany are opposed to any form of cooperation with the right-wing populists while 32% believe such decisions should be made on a case-by-case basis.

A total of 27% are generally in favor of cooperating with the AfD, most of whom are AfD supporters.

What is especially interesting in the poll, however, is the contrast between East and West Germany. The AfD has its strongholds in the East, where more people than in the West are willing to fully embrace the party: 38% want to treat the party — of which several regional chapters have been categorized as far-right extremist by the domestic intelligence agency — just like any other political group. That figure roughly corresponds to the level of support for right-wing populists in the formerly socialist East Germany (GDR).

Many AfD supporters feel marginalized

This figure also reflects the continuing shift away from "mainstream" parties. A good half of those surveyed — more than ever before in the Deutschlandtrend — support a fundamental change in German politics while only four in ten prefer isolated policy adjustments.

In other words, confidence and trust in the political system continue to wane. Forty-three percent of all respondents say they constantly feel marginalized. When this question is put to AfD supporters, that figure jumps to 70%.

The past few weeks in German politics have been marked by heated debates over proposed reforms and by a rather chaotic reshuffling of the cabinet. Even before this, approval ratings for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's policies were not high; now, only 12% believe that the new cabinet appointments will lead to better policies.

One-third are afraid of terrorism

And the latest terrorist attack in Germany has also had a significant impact on people's views. On July 25, a young Islamist from Berlin drove a rental car into a crowd during the Berlin Pride celebrations, killing one woman and seriously injuring 31 people. The following day, police shot and killed the man, who had fled after carrying out the attack. This horrific event has once again drawn attention to how vulnerable Germany is to terrorist attacks.

One-third of all respondents said they are very concerned they might become victims of terrorism themselves. Now, 70% see Islamist terrorism as the greatest threat. At the end of the last decade, on the other hand, right-wing extremist terrorism was still seen by German citizens as the greatest threat.

For the ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey in August, infratest-dimap interviewed approximately 1,300 representative German citizens between August 3 and 5.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Middle East: Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan sign defense deal
entries.summary: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a joint defense deal. According to the agreement, an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all of them. Follow DW for the latest.
entries.content:
Middle East

Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan sign defense deal

Published August 7, 2026last updated August 7, 2026

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a joint defense deal. According to the agreement, an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all of them. Follow DW for the latest.

What you need to know

  • Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a joint defense pact
  • Dozens of Yemeni troops killed in ongoing missile and drone attacks by Houthis
  • Riyadh reports 11 civilians injured after 'indiscriminate shelling against civilian objects'

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about the Middle East on Friday, August 7:

Skip next section Abu Dhabi says unprovoked attacks significantly impacting shipping operations

Abu Dhabi says unprovoked attacks significantly impacting shipping operations

The Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) said on Friday that the war in Iran is ‌significantly ⁠impacting its operations.

ADNOC said it was taking steps to protect employees, assets ‌and operations amid unprovoked ​attacks and that 15 of its vessels had ​been targeted by missiles and drones while ⁠transiting ​the Strait ​of Hormuz since the start ​of the ‌conflict.

In a press release, ADNOC said three of its ships had been attacked this week alone, reporting one employee killed and 20 injured.

ADNOC's Friday statement said, "Freedom of navigation and the safe, uninterrupted passage of commercial shipping through international waterways must be respected and protected without threat, harassment or attack."

Skip next section Rheinmetall says it will take years to replenish US ATACMS stockpiles

Rheinmetall says it will take years to replenish US ATACMS stockpiles

Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger on Friday said it would take time to ramp up planned ATACMS missile production with US partner Lockheed Martin, highlighting the difficulty of replenishing weapons stockpiles depleted by President Donald Trump's decision to launch a war against Iran.

The US has reportedly burnt through much of its stockpile of long-range precision missiles during the five-month conflict with Iran, further raising concerns about its military readiness for future crises.

Trump on Thursday played down a Reuters report this week on US weapons shortages, claiming Washington has an "almost unlimited" supply of some munitions while acknowledging stocks of others were lower.

Last month, Rheinmetall — Europe's largest ammunition maker — signed a memorandum of understanding with US arms maker Lockheed Martin — the world's largest defense contractor— to jointly produce Army Tactical ​Missile Systems (ATACMS) at Rheinmetall's Unterluess plant in northern Germany, where production facilities are scheduled to be set up next year.

"Naturally, there will also be sufficient capacity to replenish the US military arsenals depleted by the conflict involving Iran," CEO Armin Papperger told Reuters, adding the caveat: "That won't happen in two years. It will take much ‌longer."

Papperger said the ATACMS joint venture still requires approval, but noted the process was well advanced and had the backing of the US ⁠government.

Rheinmetall and Lockheed intend to target the global ATACMS market, with Papperger saying, "There will be ​a market for missiles for the next 15 years."

Skip next section Federation of German Industries says Iran war weighing heavy on global economy

Federation of German Industries says Iran war weighing heavy on global economy

The Federation of German Industries (BDI), published its latest data on global economic performance on Friday, illustrating how the war in Iran is harming outlooks.

The conflict the US and Israel started on February 28 will ultimately slow global business to 3% in 2026, the BDI said in its annual economic forecast.

BDI analysts said that the war, global growth would have been between 3.3% and 3.4%, but warn that outlooks could grow considerably more grim should the US and Iran fail to resolve the ongoing crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

The BDI's number charted different regions experiencing varying degrees of impact, with the US economy — buoyed slightly by heavy investment in AI — expected to grow by 2%, Europe by 0.8%, and China by 4.6%.

Additionally, the BDI warned of a "stagflation shock,' saying the six-month war will not only drag down growth by half a percentage point, but also drive up global inflation by a full percentage point to 4.5%.

Skip next section Iranian lawmaker warns Saudis that new pact cannot protect kingdom

Iranian lawmaker warns Saudis that new pact cannot protect kingdom

Iranian lawmaker Ebrahim Rezaei on Friday warned Saudi Arabia that its new security pact would be of little help.

"Saudis must know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as years of one-sided nursing to the Americans did not bring them security," wrote Rezaei, who is also a member of Iran's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, adding, "Reform your policies so that you do not need to beg for security from others."

Skip next section Oil prices, stock markets on roller-coaster after apparent collapse of Hormuz negotiations

Oil prices, stock markets on roller-coaster after apparent collapse of Hormuz negotiations

Oil and stocks had another roller-coaster day on Friday with markets steady and oil slightly lower in Europe, and stocks retreating as oil prices rose in the US. 

Stock and oil markets had been buoyed slightly this week by hopes that a promised US-Iran agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz would become reality and increase the flow of fuel and goods through the waterway.

Mirroring the hope and disappointment surrounding the strait conflict, the price for benchmark Brent crude rose almost 4% on Thursday before dropping 0.3% to $83.26  on Friday morning — down from $113 earlier in the war and significantly higher than $72 a barrel prior to it.

Skip next section Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia sign defense pact in Mecca

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia sign defense pact in Mecca

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia sealed a historic defense pact on Friday, signing an agreement "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression."

"The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement," read a joint statement, reflects "a shared commitment to further strengthening collective security."

A Turkish official cited by Reuters said the agreement was purely defensive in nature and open to any regional neighbors who might want to sign on.

The official said the pact does not replace or negate previous bilateral or multilateral agreements between signatories, nor is it directed at any one actor or threat.

The agreement was signed in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Paksitan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

All three parties to the deal are Sunni-majority Muslim countries, and Pakistan is a nuclear power.

Skip next section Ships passing through Hormuz down to eight on Thursday

Ships passing through Hormuz down to eight on Thursday

Maritime intelligence provider Kpler said that only eight ships passed through the contested Strait of Hormuz on Thursday.  

That number is down from a daily average of 13 last week, and down from more than 100 a day prior to US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28.

Last week's better numbers relied on a framework agreement between the US and Iran that saw a slight respite from hostilities.

But the collapse of the agreement, as well as renewed blockades, have again brought global shipping to a standstill.

"Dry bulk traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has been cut roughly in half following the renewed blockade," wrote shipping services provider AXSMarine on X.

Though Iran wields leverage over the strait, satellite images show the US blockade of Iranian ports is also having an impact.

According to shipping data provider Windward, it has been weeks since any ships have docked at Tehran's key oil export hub Kharg Island.

Skip next section Iran-backed Houthis kill dozens of Yemeni troops in ongoing attacks — reports

Iran-backed Houthis kill dozens of Yemeni troops in ongoing attacks — reports

Iran-backed Houthi rebels killed scores of Yemeni government troops in missile and drone attacks on Thursday and Friday, with France's AFP reporting 61 soldiers dead in multiple attacks. 

A rebel spokesman said the attacks were in response to increased Saudi Arabian military support for Yemen's internationally recognized government and its forces.

Saudi Arabia's military backing of the Yemenis since 2015 and alliance with the US have marked it for attack by both the Houthis and Iran.

Thursday's ballistic missile and drone attacks injured dozens of troops beyond the 58 reported dead, in what Yemeni military sources called the worst attack on troops since 2022.

The Yemeni Ministry of Defense said in a statement that a military response would come, "at the appropriate place and time."

Thursday's attack occurred amid a series of air assaults, including one that wounded 11 civilians in the Najran region.

On Friday, three more troops were killed and four more injured when Houthis targeted Yemeni soldiers in Marib province.

The Red Sea and Yemen have become more hotly contested than ever since the Houthis leaned into the US-Iran war, helping Tehran leverage the situation in the Strait of Hormuz — and its impact on the global economy.

The expected joint defense agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan is a direct response to the changing security situation in the broader Middle East.

Skip next section Houthi militia attack wounds 11 in Saudi Arabia

Houthi militia attack wounds 11 in Saudi Arabia

An attack by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis late on Thursday wounded 11 civilians in southern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border, a military official said.

The attack injured seven Saudis, two Egyptians, a Yemeni and a Pakistani, according to General Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's government against the Shiite Houthi rebels.

He accused the rebels of "using indiscriminate shelling against civilian objects."

Neither the militia or Iran immediately responded to the coalition's statement.

Tehran has targeted Saudi Arabia since the US-Iran war started this February, as its regional archrival hosts US military facilities. Less then three weeks ago, the Houthi militants in Yemen declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, signaling that Riyadh's long-running conflict with the Houthis in Yemen is becoming increasingly intertwined with the wider Middle East war. 

Skip next section Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan to sign defense deal, sources say

Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan to sign defense deal, sources say

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan were expected to sign a defense agreement in Jeddah on Friday amid escalating tensions in the Middle East, Reuters and AFP reported, citing unnamed sources.

The pact was "under discussion for a long time," but recent developments in the region accelerated efforts to finalize it, a source close to the Saudi military told AFP.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was due to meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in the Saudi Arabian city. 

Erdogan was set to arrive on Friday, while Sharif and Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir had already arrived in the kingdom on Thursday.

In 2025, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan — the only Muslim-majority country armed with nuclear weapons — announced a joint defense deal.
